World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Law breaking drivers to be targeted amid horror year on Queensland roads
World.content:
Queensland police have launched a rolling year-round road safety operation in a bid to boost their presence and visibility on the roads as they target law breaking drivers.

It comes after the ABC last year revealed a sharp drop in road safety enforcement hours from police in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The operation, dubbed Interpose, began on Saturday and is rolling out amid another horror year on Queensland roads, with 98 lives lost as of Thursday last week.

Operation Interpose will run between the four major road safety campaigns that are usually underway during the school holidays.

Rule-breaking drivers to be targeted

Chief Superintendent Mark Wheeler said the launch of Interpose meant there would be an "operational focus" on road safety for the entirety of the year.

Qld annual road toll reaches 16-year high More than 300 people have died on Queensland roads this year, with four additional deaths already recorded over the Christmas period.

It will also ensure rule-breaking drivers are targeted outside of peak travel periods.

"We acknowledge since COVID-19, particularly at the peak of the pandemic, we did have to cease certain road safety operations," Chief Superintendent Wheeler told the ABC.

"We saw a corresponding decrease in those enforcement and other road safety activities over a period of time.

"So, what we realised was that the best way that we can try to bring down the lives lost is to make sure that we've got high visibility operations occurring."

Chief Superintendent Mark Wheeler says the high-visibility operation will help curb road deaths. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

In 2019, the last full calendar year before the COVID pandemic struck, police logged 890,728 road safety enforcement hours.

But by 2024 this had fallen to 478,143 hours, reflecting a 46 per cent drop over the five-year period.

The number of lives lost on Queensland roads, meanwhile, climbed from a record low of 220 in 2019 to 302 in 2024.

"I think when we saw the decrease in that enforcement in that road safety operational tempo, we certainly saw an increase in road trauma," Chief Superintendent Wheeler acknowledged.

"And that's not just in the fatalities, but also in injury crashes.

"Also compounding this challenge is that Queensland is a growing state. We know since 2019, there are at least half a million more licenced drivers on our roads."

Police hours on the road climbing

In 2025, there was an upswing in police hours on the road, with 522,968 hours dedicated towards traffic enforcement.

As of March 31 this year, police had logged 129,976 hours — putting them on track for a similar number of hours to last year.

Chief Superintendent Wheeler said he believed Operation Interpose would help lift those enforcement hours.

"There was a period of time undoubtedly that the general public felt that there weren't many police out there, so you could take more risks," he said.

" You could speed, you could have a few drinks at the pub and still drive home. Well, we're here to tell you, you can't do that. "

Police are planning to use all road safety strategies during the operation.

The operation will involve high-visibility techniques including patrols, random breath testing, and speed detection equipment. (Supplied: QPS)

This includes high visibility patrols, random breath testing, and the deployment of speed detection equipment.

"For the entirety of the year, there will be an operational focus," Chief Superintendent Wheeler warned.

"Really, really focused, intelligence led, information from our districts, information from our regions, as to where we need to be deploying our resources."

The other operations run during the holiday periods are called Mistletoe, Easter Break, Cold Snap, and Spring Break.

In 2025, Queensland's road toll came to 306, which was five more deaths than the year before.

World.title: More families are sleeping in cars. But they're not the highest housing priority
World.content:
Erin* faced a situation that's the worst fear for many Tasmanians: their private rental ending without a lease renewal.

She applied for dozens of rental properties, but when that didn't work, she was placed on a waiting list for the shelters in the area.

But with two teenage children, it was impossible to find anywhere.

They lived in their car for several months.

"Their mental and physical health is suffering," a new report from Anglicare Tasmania reads.

"[Her daughter] feels embarrassed and it's getting harder to go to school at all."

They are far from alone.

In 2025, there were 87 people with dependent children who presented to Anglicare Tasmania who had no housing whatsoever; of those, 37 were living in motor vehicles, 21 in tents and 21 were in improvised structures.

It's likely to be an under-estimate, and it represents a worsening trend that Anglicare picked up as part of an analysis of 12 months of data for people accessing Housing Connect front door services in Tasmania.

An increasing number of families are moving into larger family groups to avoid homelessness in Tasmania, creating overcrowding issues for children. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

For the year, 1,431 parents with 4,237 dependent children sought urgent housing support.

That was 19 per cent more children compared with the 12 months to June 2025.

Almost all of the increase was seen in the state's north-west and south.

Anglicare Tasmania policy and advocacy officer Rebecca Forbes said families sleeping in cars and tents were just a small proportion of those facing imminent need.

"They could be couch surfing, staying with relatives, staying somewhere they can't afford or somewhere really overcrowded just to keep a roof over their head," Ms Forbes said.

" They might not be in crisis accommodation because they're trying to keep their family together. "

These more hidden forms of homelessness continue to increase Tasmania, adding to the developmental risks for children.

'I sleep on the ground': Overcrowding continues

In another instance, a Tasmanian family spoke of their experiences of couch surfing with another family.

"[My brother] sleeps on the couch, and I sleep on the ground on a mattress. She [younger sister] sleeps next to me."

This is also a growing trend.

Housing shortage leads to overcrowding for families Tasmania's public housing overcrowding rates are higher than the national average and continue to grow, with one family in Hobart's northern suburbs given priority status still waiting after four years.

While 82 per cent of people with dependent children who sought urgent housing support were "housed", their housing was often insecure.

Of those, 41 per cent were not on a lease.

This included 260 families who were couch surfing, 72 in boarding houses or paying relatives to live with them, and 78 who were living with relatives for free.

Anglicare's Housing Connect front door data showed that 1,300 children lived in families with more than six members, and 600 were living in family groups of 10 people or more.

Rebecca Forbes, from Anglicare Tasmania's social action and research centre, says families are having to make "impossible" choices in Tasmania. (Supplied: Anglicare Tasmania)

Ms Forbes said these living situations could have a lasting impact on children.

"If you're living in the lounge room, for example, you might have to pack up your stuff every night," she said.

"If you're sharing a room with multiple other kids of different ages, you're unlikely to be sleeping well, you probably have nowhere to do your homework.

" You're never able to relax and be a kid, which means you get to school and you're really tired or you've got a short fuse, that's a huge stress often on children. "

'Priority' status increasingly competitive

Family violence remains a common factor.

It was listed as the main reason in 19 per cent of presentations which involved dependent children — more than three times the rate for people without children.

Loading...

Ms Forbes said some Tasmanians were having to make "impossible" choices, such as remaining with a family violence perpetrator due to a lack of options.

"A lot of crisis accommodation isn't designed with families in mind ... there might be no crisis accommodation available, none nearby, or none that can house the whole family," Ms Forbes said.

"If you've got multiple children, if you've got older children, as a parent you may well be wanting to do what you can to keep them in more of a home-like environment, like staying with family and friends, even if it's really overcrowded."

Anglicare Tasmania has found that people with dependent children are often doing all they can to avoid homelessness, or ending up in shelters. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

People with children seeking housing in critical situations — including family violence, sleeping in cars or tents, or severe overcrowding — were not granted the highest priority.

Instead, they are deemed "standard priority" or "general need".

The highest priority was granted to people exiting institutional care settings or a health facility into homelessness, which is also a significant cohort in Tasmania.

Child was left homeless due to child protection delays A 13-year-old boy was left languishing in a homeless shelter for months because of Tasmanian child protection department's "gross negligence", a family member says.

But Ms Forbes said these categorisations meant families fell through the gaps.

"A lot of these families aren't coming from crisis or homelessness accommodation because the parents are trying to keep their kids in as normal an environment as possible," Ms Forbes said.

"Which means that they are still in great need but they're not in that category of coming from a shelter."

Family violence housing not specific cohort

Tasmania used to have a standalone family violence rapid rehousing program, but that was then combined with the private rental incentive scheme.

Ms Forbes said this meant that the housing available for people fleeing family violence was also available for those of the highest priority.

"It's not a ring-fenced group in the same way that it was," she said.

In one case — detailed in the report — it took nine weeks for a mother to get housing in the scheme.

In the meantime, she slept in her car while her children stayed with an aunt.

Government's lofty ambitions not being met

The Tasmanian government has lofty goals when it comes to its housing targets.

This includes a 20-year ambition where "everyone has a safe, warm home, one that protects health and gives stability to build a great life".

Dozens of families with dependent children were sleeping in cars or tents in Tasmania in 2025. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Housing is also enshrined as a "fundamental human right" in the Homes Tasmania Act.

But the front door homelessness data from Anglicare shows that the state was moving away from these goals, Ms Forbes said.

"The data is showing that this is getting harder for more people and that we are going to need to do more to reduce the impacts, particularly on children," she said.

" It's not the foundations that we want for kids in our community. "

Anglicare Tasmania recommended that families escaping family violence should be prioritised for rapid access to housing, even if they were not living in a shelter.

Other recommendations included extending school-based support for children in housing insecurity, increasing social and affordable housing stock to meet demand, and increasing crisis and transitional housing for victim-survivors of family violence.

Tasmanian Housing Minister Kerry Vincent said the cost of living has made things more difficult for Tasmanians and that additional social housing was being provided.

"Crisis accommodation is intended to provide short-term, safe and immediate accommodation for people in urgent need," Mr Vincent said.

"It supports thousands of Tasmanians every year, and we will continue to increase the capacity of crisis accommodation facilities right around the state.

"Beyond crisis accommodation facilities, Housing Connect may arrange brokered accommodation for those fleeing violence."

*Name has been changed.

World.title: Street artist Peter Drew on why his 'Aussie' posters are still important
World.content:
Unlike his anonymous counterpart Banksy, Australian street artist Peter Drew has always been happy to own his vandalism.

Ten years after creating one of Australia's most recognisable street art series, Drew is still spending his days plastering posters on brick walls and decaying facades across the country.

"I know it's illegal, but I think the reason why I haven't been brought to justice is that the posters are popular," he told triple j hack.

"People don't want to prosecute me because they like them [the posters] and I put them up in places where there are ugly walls all over the city."

Loading...

Drew started the "Aussie" series in 2016 as a way of challenging assumptions about Australia's national identity.

Last year, he announced he was revising the project in an effort "to fix racism", adding five more pictures to the series.

The first picture he used, a decade ago now, was of Muslim hawker Monga Khan, who arrived in Australia in 1895.

"As soon as I saw the photograph, I knew that was the guy," he said.

" He looks majestic and mysterious, and I knew he was going to be the hero of this project. "

'It's so special'

Over the past decade, the series has expanded to include other archival pictures of ethnically and culturally diverse people, with the word 'Aussie' displayed prominently underneath.

Drew has been putting up 'Aussie' posters for 10 years. (triple j hack: Angel Parsons)

Drew estimates he has put up 5,000 posters in communities across Australia — all hand-printed and coloured by him.

"I've tried to get out to smaller communities, but not enough because I'm doing it all myself," he said.

"It's entirely self funded. I've had plenty of offers to partner up with government … but I just like being on my own and not having to be accountable.

"This way, everyone knows that if they see a poster and they have supported the project, they have actually helped it happen."

The pictures he reproduces come from the national archives, which means he often does not know much about the people he is spotlighting.

"Sometimes descendants will reach out and it's super exciting," he said.

"I get so much information, and that part of it is so special to me."

'A counterpoint to xenophobia'

Originally inspired by the cameleers who were crucial in opening up Outback Australia in the 1800s, the idea for the poster series came to Drew in 2016, at a time he said was not too dissimilar to now.

"When I started this project, there was this huge wave of anti-Islamic sentiment.

"I thought this history would be a great counterpoint to that xenophobia which was on the street."

One of Drew's popular 'Aussie' posters on a wall in Sydney. (triple j hack: Angel Parsons)

Despite the popularity of the posters leading him to write a book, grow a social media following and sell his work online, Drew admitted not everyone was a fan.

He said that at times, he has been attacked or verbally abused while putting up his work.

"I don't want to make someone that angry," he said.

"Usually after a few minutes, they're embarrassed, and it dissipates pretty quickly."

More recently, the Aussie series was hijacked in Melbourne.

A copycat poster started appearing across the city in the same style as Drew's work, but featuring a picture of the alleged Bondi gunman, Naveed Akram.

"There's a real sort of angry nihilism to it," Drew said.

"They're not doing that out of love for Australia, are they?

"They're just wanting to get under people's skin."

Sparking conversations

Drew said the most rewarding part of the project has been the conversations it has started with so many people across Australia.

He said curiosity often led to a more nuanced discussion.

"Someone will say, 'who is that guy? Doesn't look very Aussie to me.'

"Then I start to talk about this history, and by the end of the conversation, they can see a different perspective and understand it's all good intentions."

Loading Instagram content

The artist said he was surprised by how many people resonate with the theme — even if they don't resemble the people on the posters.

"Recently, I met a couple from Ukraine, and despite there being no Ukrainians in the Aussie poster series, they got it.

" They just really appreciated seeing somebody who doesn't fit the norm being included in Aussie. "

While he admitted he likes getting under people's skin, Drew said his intention was never for those he wants to feel accepted to be made to feel targeted.

"I've been doing this for a long time, so I've got a pretty good instinct about where to put the posters."

Expanding the Aussie concept

Ten years on, Drew believed the series is more relevant now than ever.

He has committed to continuing the Aussie project, but said that while he will never use modern images, the concept would continue to evolve.

"I'd like to include white people," he said.

Drew with one of his new posters, weighing in on the campaign to increase taxes on gas exports. (triple j hack: Angel Parsons)

"The project needs to try to depict the whole rather than just depicting the people who are excluded from the concept of Aussie.

"The way I'd like to do it is by using mugshots."

He is also exploring other themes that he said are relevant to Australians, including pushing for a tax on gas exports.

Defining an Aussie

When asked about those who call him a criminal or say his work is divisive, Drew laughed.

"They come down in the rain!" he said.

"If it didn't upset anybody, then it wouldn't really have any bite to it.

"But to be honest, I still want to win over those people who don't agree with my work."

Drew started putting up 'Aussie' posters in 2016. (ABC)

He said people often asked him what he believes makes an Aussie, and he always answered by referencing a speech made by former prime minister Bob Hawke in 1988.

"He said 'the commitment is all. The commitment to Australia is the only thing needed to be a true Australian'.

"I really hope that idea doesn't slip away."

As for how long he will keep sneaking around Australia's streets, Drew said you can expect to keep spotting his Aussie posters for at least another decade.

"I came to street art before politics, and I don't see any reason to stop.

"I really like the idea of being old and decrepit and still putting out the posters.

"So I'll keep doing this as long as I'm physically able."

World.title: AI is helping rangers protect Victorian wildlife in a fraction of the time
World.content:
When Erin Nash returned to the office with 73 field cameras from the Otways earlier this year, there were 39,000 images that needed to be sorted and analysed.

The Parks Victoria conservation officer had been monitoring how the summer bushfires affected native animals that live in the ranges, including potoroos, bandicoots and swamp antechinus.

"What we're doing is looking for where we have pockets of threatened species that have survived the fire so that we can target our feral animal control programs to give them … the best chance of survival," Dr Nash said.

Dr Erin Nash installs one of Parks Victoria's field cameras in an area of the Otways burnt by a bushfire. (Supplied: Parks Victoria)

Checking those images one by one would usually take weeks.

But within a matter of hours, Dr Nash was able to confirm a serious problem.

"These areas used to be thick with vegetation that used to prevent deer and pigs penetrating into some of our national parks," she said.

"I was able to quickly detect where we have a threat of red deer entering burnt areas, and I have already sent that intel over to deer control contractors."

The quick result was due to a new artificial intelligence tool developed by Dr Nash and her Parks Victoria colleague Mary Thorpe, along with Dutch data scientist and world-leading expert on automated wildlife recognition, Peter van Lunteren.

The species recognition model uses high-speed AI to process 20 images per second and can identify animals at greater than 95 per cent accuracy.

"It's a massive game changer for us, both in terms of time and money, and both can be reinvested back into conservation," Dr Nash said.

AI tool helps get rangers back on the ground

Thousands of cameras are set up across the state each year by Parks Victoria rangers to monitor vulnerable and endangered species, and detect and respond to feral animal threats.

But the motion detection cameras are also triggered by things such as falling leaves.

Parks Victoria has deployed field cameras across the state. (Supplied: Parks Victoria)

Dr Nash said the cameras generated millions of images, which all needed to be checked to see whether they included any animals to be identified.

She said there were often lengthy backlogs.

Other AI recognition programs existed, but they had not been trained specifically for Australian fauna.

Mr van Lunteren began working on a new AI system for Parks Victoria while living in a van on a year-long backpacking trip around Australia.

Peter van Lunteren began building AddaxAI while spending a year in Australia. (Supplied: Parks Victoria)

"If a model can take care of the bulk sorting, ecologists get to focus on what they're good at — interpreting results, making decisions and doing fieldwork," he said.

"My hope is that eventually every region has a model trained on local species and conditions."

To train the system, five million images were provided by 18 Victorian research and conservation organisations that also used remote wildlife cameras known as "camera traps", including Zoos Victoria, Phillip Island Nature Parks, Dja Dja Wurrung Clans Aboriginal Corporation, the University of Melbourne and Deakin University.

The system can now identify more than 200 native and feral species.

"The world of camera trap AI is just a really collaborative world," Mr van Lunteren said.

"It's a really nice world to work in because everybody's so friendly and everybody's sharing models and data. It's just amazing."

The AI tool identifies a long-nosed potoroo captured on camera in the Otway Ranges. (Supplied: Parks Victoria)

Dr Nash said the tool allowed Parks Victoria to respond to threats and other issues in a fraction of the time.

"Previously, feral pig images may have been on hard drives sitting there waiting for someone to analyse them for many months.

"By the time you find the pig in amongst hundreds of thousands of [images of] swamp wallabies, it's too late."

Parks Victoria says the AI tool will allow a faster response to pests and other threats. (Supplied: Parks Victoria)

Parks Victoria's Chief Conservation Scientist Mark Norman said the system was helping capture nocturnal species, animals that were difficult to locate because of their propensity to avoid humans, as well as wildlife camouflaged in the bush.

"It's better than the human eye," Dr Norman said.

"There's an animal in this photograph that none of us would have spotted except for this program," he said, referring to the camera trap image below.

Before: An image captured on a Parks Victoria field camera. . . After: An image from the same camera two seconds later when the AI tool identified a bird was in the shot. . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE An image captured on a Parks Victoria field camera. / An image from the same camera two seconds later when the AI tool identified a bird was in the shot.

The "trap" consists of the pole featuring three spoons which contain peanut butter, oats and honey to lure animals to the camera.

"This is what the computer program said was an animal," he said pointing to the detection frame in the second image.

"Based on those little markings, they allowed us to confidently identify it as an eastern ground parrot, which is one of our endangered parrots."

The rangers matched the feather patterns in the AI frame to an eastern ground parrot. (File; Supplied: National Parks NSW, Lachlan Hall)

" When you think about somebody going through 10,000 slides over three weeks, trying to find it ... this is huge. "

Dr Norman said rangers would now have more time to action threatened species programs and carry out feral animal control.

Chief Conservation Officer Mark Norman says the AI program has the capacity for further advances. (Supplied: Parks Victoria)

"People's hair will turn from grey back to their normal colour compared with the workload they used to have because it was such a strain."

Dr Norman said he hoped the program could be further developed to provide instant notifications to conservation teams, particularly when predators are detected.

Zoos Victoria has begun using the AI model, and is already putting Dr Norman's vision into action in its Lowland Leadbeater's possum safe haven program at Haining Farm in the Yarra Valley.

Arabella Eyre, the acting general manager of the zoo's Threatened Species team, said by attaching a mini-computer to the field camera, she could receive a text message alert if a cat or fox entered the area.

"We'll be able to respond quickly and get that cat or fox out of the predator exclusion fenced areas," Ms Eyre said.

" So it will really speed up the response time which will help us better protect the threatened species that would otherwise be at risk of predation. "

Ms Eyre said the model was "top of the line" at recognising species only found in south-east Australia, but she said there was potential for improvements if camera technologies evolved.

"It's pretty perfect, like it's as good as it's going to get with our current technology," she said.

"What's probably the next development is actually looking at how we can have cameras that take better photos and then based on better images, we'll be able to refine models."

Conservation community welcomes open source model

From today, Parks Victoria has made the AI recognition model available to the community as an open source program.

Dr Nash said pre-existing AI systems were operated by large tech companies.

"They then own your data," she said.

"Lots of researchers and land managers want to keep control of their underlying data."

Parks Victoria says its AI tool is free for the community to use and the ownership of photos and other data remains with the user. (Supplied: Parks Victoria)

Ms Eyre said open source was particularly important for Zoos Victoria as it eliminated the risk of vulnerable conservation information falling into the wrong hands.

"[The Parks Victoria model] is not only open source, but it also runs on your computer rather than in the cloud, which increases data security which is particularly relevant for our threatened species or species that are at risk of poaching," she said.

Mr van Lunteren said it was being offered free of charge.

"It's open source and there are no licensing costs, the data is private, you run it on your own computer." Mr van Lunteren confirmed.

World.title: Trump says shooter's 'manifesto' shows he was a 'sick guy'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says a "manifesto" apparently written by the shooter at the White House correspondents' dinner reveals he is a "sick guy" who "hates Christians".

Several US media outlets have reported on the existence of the manifesto, which reportedly states the shooter wanted to target administration officials, and was sent to the suspect's family members just before the attack.

The suspect has been identified Cole Tomas Allen, a 31-year-old teacher and engineer from Torrance, south of Los Angeles. Police were searching properties in the area on Sunday, local time.

Loading...

"The guy is a sick guy," Mr Trump told Fox News during an on-air phone interview.

"When you read his manifesto, he hates Christians. That's one thing for sure. He hates Christians, a hatred.

"And I think his sister or his brother actually was even complaining about it. You know, they were even complaining to law enforcement. So he was a very troubled guy."

Loading...

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the shooter "sought to assassinate the president and kill as many top Trump administration officials as possible".

"What was supposed to be a fun night at the [White House Correspondents' Association] dinner with President Trump delivering jokes and celebrating free speech was hijacked by a depraved crazy person," she wrote on X.

Suspect's brother alerted police: reports

Fox and CNN, citing unnamed sources, reported they had confirmed some details of the manifesto, including that it stated the shooter wanted to target Trump officials.

Fox also reported that the White House had said Mr Allen's brother had notified police in Connecticut about the manifesto.

Earlier, acting US attorney-general Todd Blanche said investigators had searched multiple properties, spoken to people who knew the suspect and found "writings" on devices connected to him.

"It does appear that he did, in fact, set out to target folks that work in the administration, likely including the president," Mr Blanche told NBC's Meet the Press program.

Guests take cover after hearing gunshots at the White House correspondents' dinner. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

Mr Banche said it appeared the shooter had travelled from Los Angeles to Washington, DC by train via Chicago.

He checked in at the Washington Hilton, which was hosting the dinner, in the past day or two.

"We believe that the two firearms he had on him, he had purchased within the past couple of years," Mr Blanche said.

'Brave agent' shot in chest

Allen is expected to be formally charged on Monday morning, local time, in federal court in Washington.

He will initially be charged with assaulting a federal officer and discharging a firearm during that assault, Mr Blanche said, but further charges are possible.

The incident, the third apparent assassination attempt on Mr Trump, has again raised questions about the president's security.

This was one of the most vulnerable moments ever for a US government ABC Americas editor was inside the ballroom when a shooting suspect was stopped by the Secret Service.

But administration officials have praised the Secret Service and others who stopped the shooter from getting into the room, where many of Trump's cabinet members and more than 2,000 guests were dining.

"We have to learn from what happened last night, and we will," Mr Blanche said.

"But the first takeaway, the takeaway that should be obvious, is that the system worked and that we stopped this suspect."

Nobody was seriously injured in the attack. But Ms Leavitt said a "brave agent took a bullet to the chest".

"President Trump was truly fearless, but as he said last night, this political violence needs to end," she said.

World.title: How dinner with the president descended into chaos
World.content:
Thousands of influential players in Washington filed into a ballroom with the US president. Then shots rang out.

Hours before Donald Trump was due to give his first address at the annual White House Correspondents' Association dinner as US president, his press secretary Karoline Leavitt promised it would be a night to remember.

"He is ready to rumble," she said in an interview with Fox News.

"It'll be funny. It'll be entertaining. There will be some shots fired, tonight, in the room."

Her lighthearted remarks turned out to be prescient.

Live: Trump likely target of shooting at correspondents' dinner, official says US Acting Attorney-General Todd Blanche says the shooter apprehended at the White House correspondents' dinner was likely targeting Donald Trump. Follow live.

Less than 20 minutes after Mr Trump took his seat, Secret Service agents were ushering him out of the room after a shooter crashed the venue armed with multiple guns and knives.

Gunshots were heard just outside the ballroom where the gala was taking place — and within seconds the suspect was arrested.

But in the aftermath, many correspondents have asked how the gunman got so close to the US president in the first place.

The red carpet arrivals

The White House Correspondents' Association dinner is an annual event celebrating the press corps that covers the US president day in, day out.

Each year about 2,500 journalists, politicians, media executives and other influential players file into the ballroom of the Washington Hilton hotel — the largest such space in the city.

But this year was notable because Mr Trump was making his first appearance as US president, after boycotting the event in previous years.

From 6pm, local time, the guests started arriving on the red carpet.

Mr Trump's top aides and cabinet secretaries filed down the red carpet in a stream — Vice-President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, high-level staffers Stephen Miller and Dan Scavino.

Other members of Trump's cabinet at the gala included Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, Education Secretary Linda McMahon and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

Considering the ballroom was filled with some of the most powerful and influential people in the United States — arguably the world — guests later said the security seemed lacking.

"All I needed was … a ticket to the White House Correspondents' Association dinner [to get in]," said ABC News Americas editor John Lyons, who attended the event.

"I took my passport and everything along thinking it's going to be high security. I arrived at the Washington Hilton. I got into the gate just by showing this [ticket]."

After the event, the UK Telegraph's chief Washington correspondent Connor Stringer wrote: "Upon arriving at the Hilton, I had remarked to a colleague just how light the measures had been. No ID checks. No pat-downs on entry. A simple flash of a cardboard ticket, which was the exact same from last year's event, was all that was needed to enter."

The BBC's chief North America correspondent Gary O'Donoghue said he was waved down with a metal detector, but said the agent "wasn't particularly interested in the bleeps set off by the contents of my inside jacket pocket".

"In short, the security felt like a regular White House correspondents' dinner — one without the sitting president in attendance," he wrote.

Mr Trump, accompanied by his wife Melania, left the White House at about 7:53pm, just minutes before the event began.

The event starts

Inside the ballroom, hundreds of journalists, including the most high-profile and senior White House correspondents from major media outlets, were gathered and waiting for the event to begin.

At about 8:12pm, an announcement rang out over the speakers: "Ladies and gentlemen — please take your seats. The program will begin momentarily."

The guests of honour at the head table were then introduced one by one, including Ms Leavitt, several high-profile White House correspondents, and the evening's headline act, mentalist Oz Pearlman.

Then, at 8:15pm, the US Marine band began a fanfare to welcome the man of the hour.

"Ladies and gentleman, the 45th and 47th president of the United States, Donald J Trump, and first lady, Melania Trump," the announcer said.

Melania Trump, Donald Trump and journalist Weijia Jiang were seated together. ( )

CBS News senior White House correspondent Weijia Jiang spoke on the night. ( )

Melania Trump and Karoline Leavitt. ( )

Mr and Ms Trump were seated between Ms Leavitt and the head of the White House Correspondents' Association, CBS correspondent Weijia Jiang.

Mr Vance was at the same table, a few seats from the president.

After a brass band rendition of the US national anthem and an opening speech from Ms Jiang, the proceedings paused for dinner.

"We have a big night ahead, and we're going to get started now — so enjoy your dinner, and we will be back. Thank you," Ms Jiang said when concluding her opening speech at 8:23pm.

The dinner and the shots

Before long, drinks were poured and plates of salad began weaving between the tables. Music continued playing while dinner guests mingled and ate.

Pearlman, whose author profile says he is renowned for his "extraordinary mind-reading abilities", was entertaining the guests at the head table.

At 8:34pm — when Pearlman was performing a trick for Ms Leavitt and the Trumps — gunshots rang out. On a live stream of the event, the shots sounded like five bangs in quick succession.

But in that moment, many people in the room did not know what was happening.

New Yorker writer Antonia Hitchens, who attended the dinner, later wrote: "I heard what sounded like a caterer dropping a stack of plates down a flight of stairs."

Mr Trump himself later said he thought the noise was "a tray going down, many times".

Pearlman continued his trick for a few more seconds — according to Bloomberg, he was trying to guess the name of the baby Ms Leavitt is expecting — before the guests at the head table realised something was amiss.

Secret Service agents were heard shouting, "Get down! Get down!"

Security officials respond after the shooting. ( )

Guests hid under tables in the room. ( )

Guest take cover after hearing gunshots at the White House correspondents' dinner. ( )

"Before anyone had time to realise what had happened, an army of black-tie-clad secret service agents leapt to their feet, scrambling across tables and sending wine bottles flying every which way," the Telegraph wrote.

Less than a minute after the shots were first heard, Mr and Ms Trump were whisked away by Secret Service agents.

Loading...

The rest of the guests were ducking low or hiding under their tables, as agents scrambled to get members of the government out of the room.

"FBI Director Kash Patel was on the floor with the rest of us — shielding his girlfriend — as a Secret Service agent ran across the ballroom to his aid," O'Donoghue later wrote.

The shooting

Outside the ballroom, a 31-year-old man from California had charged a security checkpoint armed with multiple weapons and sprinted towards the ballroom.

"He was fast. He was like a blur on tape," Mr Trump later said.

Loading...

Police said the man was armed with a handgun, a shotgun and several knives.

The suspect stormed the checkpoint with "a firearm in his hand", Interim DC Police Chief Jeffrey Carroll said, while the FBI and other witnesses said the man was carrying a "long gun".

A blurry security tape posted to social media by the US president showed a group of Secret Service agents and police waiting in an anteroom, as a man dressed in black sprinted past.

Multiple agents can be seen quickly drawing their guns then moving in the direction of the suspect, while more agents stream into the room.

The exact number of shots fired, and the precise sequence of events, has not been confirmed by police.

Guests later said they heard between three and six gunshots from just outside the main ballroom.

Security reacted quickly once the shooter emerged. ( )

The shooter was detained before reaching the ballroom. ( )

But several US media outlets reported that the shooting took place on the level above the ballroom, where a security checkpoint for the gala was located.

"It was on another floor, up some stairs and several sets of security away," CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs wrote on X.

According to the New York Times, the man was apprehended as he approached a staircase leading into the ballroom.

Veteran CNN anchor Wolf Blitzer, who had nipped up the stairs to use the bathroom, found himself just "a few feet away" from the gunman when the shooting started.

"All of a sudden I heard these loud, very loud, very scary gunshots right near me. Next thing I knew, a police officer threw me to the ground and was on top of me," he said.

"I did see the gunman on the ground after he started shooting. Police officers threw him to the ground but he was still shooting."

No injuries were reported but one Secret Service agent was shot at, saved only by his bulletproof vest.

"He [the agent] was shot from very close distance with a very powerful gun — and the vest did the job," Mr Trump later said.

According to Carroll the suspect was "pulled … to the ground and handcuffed" but not shot.

He was later identified by US media outlets as Cole Tomas Allen, a 31-year-old who lives in Torrance, California.

'The show will go on'

Police have not yet revealed how a man armed with so many weapons managed to get so far into the building.

Citing law enforcement officials, Jacobs reported that "because the Washington Hilton's hotel and other public spaces were open for other functions, the entire building wasn't secured by the Secret Service, just the specific areas where the WHCA dinner was held."

The suspect was a guest at the hotel, police said, and was believed to have acted alone.

True to form, Mr Trump was posting on social media less than an hour after being whisked out of the event.

"Quite an evening in DC," he wrote on Truth Social about 45 minutes after the shooting.

"The shooter has been apprehended, and I have recommended that we 'LET THE SHOW GO ON' but will entirely be guided by Law Enforcement."

The show did not go on.

Guests comfort one another following a shooting. ( )

A shoe, abandoned in the chaos, lies on the floor of the hotel. ( )

About two hours after the shooting unfolded, Mr Trump was back at the White House, holding a press conference.

He said he wanted the event to continue but was not permitted by his Secret Service agents.

"We wanted to stay tonight. I will tell you, I fought like hell to stay, but they [said] it was protocol," he said.

The dinner will be rescheduled for some time in the next 30 days, Mr Trump said.

And while earlier in the night Ms Leavitt flagged the US president was "ready to rumble", Mr Trump said he might tone down his planned speech when the event is held again.

"I was all set to really rip it. And I said to my people, 'This would be the most inappropriate speech ever made,'" he said in the post-shooting press conference.

"I don't know if I could ever be as rough as I was going to be tonight … I'll be very boring the next time."

World.title: 'Membership to nothing': The multi-million-dollar Wild West of rewards clubs
World.content:
Despite the flashing lights, the wads of cash and seemingly endless supply of Italian sports cars, this isn't Vegas.

It is just one of Australia's many "rewards clubs" popping up all over the country, claiming to have given away millions in prizes.

More than 80 rewards clubs have popped up over Australia, sometimes attracting hundreds of thousands of social media followers. (Supplied: LXG)

The ABC has identified more than 80 companies that run on a rewards club model, where customers pay a monthly subscription to get "free" entries into prize draws of cars, houses and cash, often worth millions of dollars.

Collectively they claim to have given away more than $220 million in prizes. Despite these businesses being run like gambling operations, the industry is almost entirely unregulated.

The range of niches is impressive.

Prizes offered range from luxury goods such as sports cars, handbags, houses and watches, to hunting equipment, Pokémon cards and heavy construction machinery.

The range of prizes offered cater to almost every type of consumer; from handbags to firearms stores vouchers. (Supplied: L.L. Collective)

The companies rely on "trade promotion" permits, which are intended to promote a product or service, and are not meant to be the product themselves, such as the McDonald's Monopoly promotion.

Importantly, entry into the draws needs to be free.

Do you know more? You can contact business reporter Jasper Wells at wells.jasper@proton.me

Whilst turning over millions in revenue, these companies face none of the stringent regulation or consumer protections that gambling operators do, such as age verification, deposit limits and the self-exclusion register.

Collectively these rewards clubs claim to have given away more than $220 million. ((Supplied: Hega))

Gambling licenses are also extremely hard to acquire and cost potentially tens of thousands of dollars, whereas almost anyone with an ABN can obtain a trade promotion permit, costing around $500 a year.

Despite being just one of 11 gaming types in New South Wales, trade promotions make up more than 80 per cent of all gaming-related complaints received by the NSW Department of Fair Trading.

In the last financial year, there were over 60 complaints relating to trade promotions.

Anoulack Chanthivong says he is very concerned by the increase in the number of complaints against trade promotions. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts )

NSW Better Regulation and Fair Trading Minister Anoulack Chanthivong said he was very concerned about the growing number of complaints, and condemned attempts to mislead consumers.

"A giveaway business isn't legal. It's either gambling or a [charity] raffle", Andreas Fung said, a director at Trade Promotions and Lotteries.

His company helps businesses genuinely trying to promote a product or service follow trade promotion rules.

"It's just become gambling," he said of some rewards clubs.

RS Rewards says it has given away more than $10 million in prizes. One of them was a $2 million luxury home on the Gold Coast. (Supplied: RS Rewards)

'A membership to nothing'

Legally, these companies are "rewards clubs" or "lifestyle clubs", boasting exclusive discounts on brands and access to events, with the entries into prize draws a "free" extra.

But for many, the "exclusive benefits" they offer are often broken links, the occasional members' event or publicly available discounts.

The star of the show is the prize draws.

Whilst these companies are legally businesses that sell a product or service, it's clear the focus is the giveaways. (Supplied: Freedom Giveaways)

"Because they don't have a business, they make up a product," Mr Fung said of rewards clubs.

" It's a membership to nothing. "

Mr Fung said he got four or five phone calls a week from people wanting to set up rewards clubs, and tried to talk them out of it.

"I convince some to give up, some go ahead with it, and some just run without a permit," he said.

Early adopter supports more regulation

Adrian Portelli, also known as "Lambo Guy" for his love of Italian sports cars, says he was the first to use the model with his company, LMCT+, which has been running as a rewards club for almost 10 years.

The company says it has given away tens of millions of dollars in prizes.

Adrian Portelli's company was the first to use the model, and has been running for almost 10 years. (Supplied: LMCT+)

When asked whether the law needed to be changed, he said, "100 per cent, I've said this from day one, there needs to be stricter laws on this".

Mr Portelli said his company was genuinely trying to give customers good value and discounts exclusive to his club, but said he wants to move away from the rewards club business model.

On Wednesday, the billionaire opened a petrol station in Melbourne, exclusive to subscribers, selling fuel for $1 per litre. The opening caused traffic chaos, leading to the police being called.

He expressed frustration at competitors trying to imitate his business model and their reckless approach to the law.

"A lot of people are trying to rip off the business and not do the right thing," Mr Portelli told ABC News in a phone call.

" They're just f***ing cowboys. They have no perception of the law. "

LMCT+ has an entire team dedicated to making sure the prize draws follow the law, Mr Portelli added.

In March, the company was found guilty of running an unlawful lottery and fined $40,000. Mr Portelli was found not guilty on related charges and said the company would appeal the ruling.

The prizes for the draws for some clubs are often worth hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars. (Supplied: LMCT+)

Fun for all ages

Unlike licensed gambling operators, there is no age verification, meaning anyone with a debit card or PayPal account can sign up to use these services.

Tucked away in the terms and conditions are small disclaimers saying that under-18s should not use the platform and are ineligible to win, but the ABC has not encountered a single website that verifies the user's age.

Some companies seem to be aware of under-18s using their platforms and encourage them to enter the prize draws.

Thomas Fu, director of Motor Culture Australia, a motoring rewards club, said, "I don't know if there are any under-18s. If they want to enter, they have to tick a box".

"If someone wants to sign up, 14 or 15 years old, they're able to sign up, but they can't win," Mr Portelli said.

He said they were using the platform for its intended purpose, which was for discounts and events.

"If I told you there wasn't anyone under the age of 18, I'd be lying," Mr Portelli said.

Even the Wild West has limits

But even lax trade promotion laws have their limits. RS Rewards, a club that claims to have given away more than $10 million in prizes, had its permit cancelled by the NSW Department of Fair Trading in March, finding the company had broken the law 29 times in 2025.

'Giveaway' club loses licence after multiple breaches of law One of Australia's biggest "giveaway" clubs has had its community gaming licence cancelled. The business has continued to run draws following the cancellation, raising questions around potentially illegal lotteries.

Despite this, the company has continued to run prize draws, collectively worth more than $1 million, promoting them to NSW residents even though they are not eligible to win.

The company's social media accounts are filled with similar stunts to the American influencer Mr Beast, who is known for theatrical stunts and giving money to loyal fans.

RS Rewards's marketing is packed with well-known influencers and former AFL players, including Brendan Fevola, who has spoken publicly about his previous gambling addiction, once losing $300,000 in a weekend.

Brendan Fevola is a featured spokesperson for RS Rewards, appearing in promotional videos and helping with the draws. (Supplied: RS Rewards)

He is now a prominent spokesperson for the company, featuring in promotional videos, the company's website, and drawing the names of winners.

RS Rewards and Fevola did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Not just a game

Whilst these businesses style themselves as a "lifestyle", their subscribers tell a different story.

The marketing and social media accounts portray the prize draws as a bit of low-stakes fun, but to plenty of customers they're anything but.

When Mr Portelli asked LMCT+'s TikTok followers what they would do with $600,000, one user wrote, "I would get a powered wheelchair [and] other equipment for my disability's [sic] to have a better quality of life".

It was just one of many similar comments on the companies' social media accounts, hoping for the chance of a financial lifeline from these prizes.

"I would pay my medical bills off and buy a house and pay the rest of my debts off," another user wrote.

The ABC has reviewed social media comments from users of these platforms, and identified dozens of people who say they are entering the prize draws to pay off medical bills, support themselves or family members with a disability, to pay off debts or who are homeless.

For some users the prizes draws are not just fun and games. (ABC News)

"They are ultimately going to hurt the consumer," Mr Fung said.

"I just think it's wrong. It's morally wrong."

"Don't like being a member, but always enter into the draws in hopes," another user said.

Calls for urgent reform

The lax regulatory environment makes prosecuting dodgy operators difficult.

Whilst there are penalties for running illegal lotteries, regulators can have a hard time proving the business is not honestly conducting a giveaway to promote a product or service, said Emma Tiberi, a lawyer from Born Legal who specialises in trade promotions.

In light of the recent action against LMCT+ and RS Rewards, Ms Tiberi said there may be "more scrutiny in this space".

Independent senator David Pocock has made strengthening gambling regulation a key issue, arguing the government needs to take a stronger stance on gambling ads and companies skirting the law.

David Pocock is calling for stronger gambling regulations. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"This is particularly concerning at a time when many people are feeling financially insecure and looking for ways to put food on the table," he previously told the ABC.

The lack of protections for consumers could have significant consequences.

Kei Sakata, an expert in gambling harm at the Australian Institute of Family Studies, warned, "users may have no transparency about net losses, fewer limits on bonus-driven spend, and no access to self‑exclusion or other harm‑reduction tools".

Every expert we talked to said the space needed more regulation and scrutiny.

Gambling repackaged for women as 'fun' and 'harmless', study finds Gambling is being promoted as fun, social and "harmless" for women through social media and lifestyle marketing, in a shift researchers warn is normalising betting and obscuring the risks.

"We are already the biggest losers in the world when it comes to per capita gambling losses and predatory companies continue to find new ways to skirt regulations and exploit loopholes to fleece Australians," Senator Pocock said.

Earlier in the month, the Albanese government announced a crackdown on "dodgy lotteries", but it is understood that this is targeting keno-style lotteries and overseas lotteries, not home-grown trade promotions.

NSW minister Mr Chanthivong said the state government was reviewing trade promotions with interstate regulators.

But for now, the difference between trade promotions and gambling rests largely on how they are classified, a gap that has proven to be durable and very lucrative.

World.title: China's 'quirky' fix for property crisis rewards marathon runners
World.content:
What do marathon runners, AI experts and tennis players have in common?

In China, they have all become the target of creative housing subsidies.

Earlier this month, a social media account for the government of Nanjing — a capital city of China in imperial times — posted that it was providing housing subsidies of up to 100,000 yuan ($20,530) to participants in the city's marathon this year.

These "exclusive runner subsidies" for buying apartments in selected properties in the Jiangsu province city would be applied on top of existing discounts.

Runners who registered for the marathon but did not participate could still get a 20,000 yuan ($4,100) subsidy and those who participated but did not finish the run could get 60,000 yuan ($12,320).

Marathons have surged in popularity across China, with nearly 600 races organised nationwide last year. (Reuters: Tingshu Wang, file)

Similar schemes have been reported in the cities of Wuxi and Yancheng in the same province, and some parts of Shaanxi province.

Separately, in central China's Hubei province, generous subsidies have been offered to attract people who have other talents, such as top tennis players and coaches, as well as AI and humanoid robotics experts.

The ABC has attempted to contact the city authorities.

Ongoing property slump

China's property industry has been in a prolonged downturn since 2016 when the government cracked down on debt-fuelled expansion and speculation to rein in overheated housing prices and improve affordability.

The tightening of financing rules led to mounting debt and the default of property giants such as Evergrande.

Associate professor Qiang Li, a property expert at Deakin Business School, said local governments were "pulling out all the stops" after years of stagnation.

"The situation remains pessimistic … in the first three months of 2026, in large cities in China, the sales volume actually dropped by about 10 per cent or more than 10 per cent," he said.

Qiang Li says China's property market is yet to bounce back. (ABC News: Kai Feng)

Data from China's National Bureau of Statistics shows prices fell for new homes across most cities in 2025.

"There are some good signs, but still the numbers are not showing an immediate recovery," Dr Li said.

"In the last 10 to 20 years, the prices have always gone up and this is the stage where we are experiencing some kind of correction … it's just we are not sure that we are at the bottom yet."

Will the incentives work?

Ghost towns have emerged in China in recent years. (Reuters: Tingshu Wang)

Marathons have been increasing in popularity in China in the last few years.

In 2025, the country hosted 594 road running events, attracting more than 1.2 million full-marathon runners and more than three million half-marathon participants.

Pan Wang, an associate professor of Chinese and Asian studies at the University of New South Wales, noted that marathons were most popular among China's middle-aged middle class, who often fought hard to secure a spot in these events.

No official data on the number of applications to the incentive programs have been released.

But Beijing's willingness to let local governments experiment with unconventional measures suggests urgency in reviving the sector.

Dr Wang said the marathon subsidies were designed to "kill several birds with one stone".

"Beyond boosting tourism and housing demand, they enhance city competitiveness and attract higher-income groups," she said.

Pan Wang says Chinese local governments hope to be "killing several birds with one stone" with the subsidies. (Supplied: UNSW)

Dr Wang described the approach as "policy innovation", noting marathon participants often had relatively strong purchasing power.

"Large sporting events can convert 'race traffic' into 'property traffic,'" she said.

Dr Li agreed the measures could help smaller cities compete with top-tier hubs such as Shanghai or Shenzhen.

"This is one way for these local governments to signal to the general public, to the whole country, that our cities are actually competitive in attracting these individuals, and this is a good place to do business," he said.

However, reports suggest some subsidies only apply to selected properties that are often in peripheral areas and struggling to find buyers.

"The gimmick value of these quirky policies outweighs the real financial benefits," Dr Wang said.

"Rather than offering genuine discounts, their primary aim is to promote the city and stimulate the local property market.

"Because these are often 'unsellable' projects, the conditions are frequently less than ideal."

She that there was no data available on how many homes had actually been sold through the schemes.

Meanwhile, Chinese sports authorities have raised concerns about excessive commercialisation.

They argue that the linking of sporting events to property promotions may distort the purpose of sports.

Could subsidies be used in Australia?

Australia is experiencing a sustained boom in property demand, in stark contrast to the prolonged downturn currently facing China. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

Dr Li said such incentives were unlikely to be of much use in Australia's larger cities, but could be useful for local governments in regional areas.

"The gateway cities [are] quite competitive, so offering some additional layers of these incentives wouldn't make a lot of difference," he said.

"But for regional towns, it could be beneficial, but the local governments will have to decide by themselves how they would manage such a program."

World.title: NRL does a good job with Anzac Day – shame about some of the jerseys
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion NRL does a good job with Anzac Day – shame about some of the jerseys Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist April 27, 2026 — 5:41am

April 27, 2026 — 5:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Anzac Day should and does warrant mixed feelings, but each year rugby league drapes it in what historian Peter Cochrane called a “magic cloak” designed to sanctify everything that it touches. Whether a football code should be getting involved in such ceremonies is a question that is always worth asking; we hear a bit too much about rugby league defenders making desperate tackles “in the Anzac spirit”. Loading That said, the NRL does a good job with pre-match formalities, including a moment of silent reflection that commemorates rather than celebrates the sacrifice. It’s a fine line. But then there are some of the special Anzac Round jerseys worn this year, which were just not good. Canberra’s had an ill-conceived camo design.



Some of the others, such as those worn by the Cowboys, Rabbitohs, Dolphins and Eels, looked like they had done heavy service in military laundries. Since the Tigers’ Anzac jersey debacle a few years ago, when a rogue image appeared in the design, clubs have been careful. Kaeo Weekes: Exciting fullback, questionable jersey. Getty Images But some of this weekend’s jerseys looked like the magic cloak had been put in a mixed wash on high temperature. The best jersey is the Dragons’, with poppies comprising the red V. The fact that it’s also slightly off – the poppies originated with Remembrance Day, not Anzac Day – is somehow fitting. Remembrance Day, after all, commemorates the wish to end war.



Spineless wonders Craig Bellamy was “the most embarrassed I’ve ever been in my footy life” after Melbourne fell 48-6 to South Sydney, their sixth straight defeat. Twice more, Bellamy used the word “embarrassing”. After 22 years of success at the Storm, now he knows how other coaches feel. Melbourne’s start to the season went from bad to worse against the Rabbitohs. Getty Images A notable feature of the Storm’s season, highlighted on Saturday night, might herald a change in orthodox rugby league thinking. Bellamy is the creator of the idea that if you get the spine of a team right, everything else will fall into place. Year after year, Melbourne has cycled through forwards and centres but sustained their success through keeping an outstanding combination of 1, 6, 7 and 9.



Melbourne still have the best spine in the competition: Sua Fa’alogo, Cameron Munster, Jahrome Hughes and Harry Grant. But the elastic might have finally snapped. To see Souths, a team with a moderate spine but brilliance across the field, their game most influenced by a lock (Cameron Murray) and a left centre (Latrell Mitchell), thrash Melbourne in this way suggests rugby league has changed fundamentally, and the spine is no longer the be-all and end-all. Ode for a tryless game Amid some one-sided games, the most disappointing of the round was the Cowboys’ nine tries to six win over Cronulla on Friday. It was reminiscent of the Boxing Day Test in the Ashes cricket series last summer: both sides simply gave up on the hard work of defence, and three tries in the last seven minutes of the match were an ignominious ending.



Related Article NRL 2026 ‘We don’t want the halcyon days of our club to be four decades ago’: Why 1986 reunion is bittersweet for Eels To call it touch football would have been an insult to touch. Forty years ago, Parramatta and Canterbury played a tryless grand final, two Mick Cronin penalty goals defeating one from Terry Lamb. It was seen as the nadir of the era of gang tackles, the day a fabulously attacking Parramatta team defeated Canterbury at their own game. Peter Sterling, at a celebration last week, said: “I challenge anyone to go back and have a look at the 80 minutes and not be excited by it.” I’m not sure everyone shared that view at the time, but sometimes today’s easy-breezy approach to defence makes you pine for the dark days of Warren Ryan’s ‘Wokball’.



Move over, Erling Haaland Code-switching is always a rugby league talking point, but it’s not often you see it in the

middle of a game. In the 24th minute of their match against Parramatta at Brookvale on Sunday, Manly’s Jason Saab was standing uncontested under a Jamal Fogarty cross-field bomb. View post on X Instead of catching it or letting it bounce, Saab deliberately headed the ball forward about 15 metres.



“Is that legal?” Andrew Voss asked in commentary, before saying to Cooper Cronk, “Can you explain why he did that?” The expert comments man replied, “I have no idea.” A clue arrived minutes later, when Saab fumbled on the first tackle. If you can’t use your hands, you can’t drop the ball. Voss, rather kindly, wondered if it was a “delayed concussion”.

World.title: ASX set for steady open, Wall Street hits records
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set for steady open, Wall Street hits records Stan Choe April 27, 2026 — 5:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

A surge for Intel following a blowout profit report led the US stock market to more records on Friday, while oil prices kept yo-yoing in the wait for what’s next with the Iran war. The S&P 500 climbed 0.8 per cent and topped its prior all-time high, which was set on Wednesday. The Dow Jones dipped 79 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 1.6 per cent to its own record thanks to the jump for tech. Another day of bumper results drove Wall Street higher despite ongoing uncertainty over the Iran war. AP The Australian sharemarket is set for a flat open, with futures on Saturday pointing to a fall of 3 points at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.36 at 5.15am AEST. Intel led the way and roared past its 2000 peak during the dot-com boom to an all-time high. It soared 23.6 per cent for its best day since 1987 after reporting much stronger results for the first three months of the year than analysts expected. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the next wave of artificial-intelligence technology is increasing the need for Intel’s chips and products, and the company’s forecast for profit in the spring topped analysts’ estimates.



Related Article Opinion

Inflation Coles and Woolies need to eat some of the food price rise pain Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Such strong profit reports have helped Wall Street rally to records, and the S&P 500 has leaped nearly 13 per cent in a little under a month. Hopes have also built in financial markets that the United States and Iran can find a way to avoid a worst-case scenario for the global economy because of their war. A ceasefire is tenuously in place between the two, but tensions between them are still keeping oil tankers from passing through the Strait of Hormuz to deliver crude from the Persian Gulf to customers worldwide. Oil prices climbed this week on worries about the strait, but an encouraging signal came Friday after Iran’s top diplomat said he was heading to Pakistan. That’s where officials have been trying to get the United States and Iran to convene for a second round of ceasefire negotiations. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt later said in an interview on Fox News Channel that President Donald Trump is sending his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Pakistan to meet with Iran’s foreign minister.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude to be delivered in June yo-yoed for much of the day before settling at $US105.33, up 0.2 per cent. The price for a barrel of Brent oil delivered in July, which is where more of the trading is happening in the market, fell 0.2 per cent to $US99.13. On Wall Street, Procter & Gamble rose 2.5 per cent after reporting stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said it saw broad-based growth across regions and products, which include Bounty paper towels and Tide detergent. That helped offset a drop of 25.5 per cent for Charter Communications, whose profit for the latest quarter came in weaker than analysts expected. It lost 120,000 internet customers during the three months, more than some analysts expected. Hartford Insurance Group fell 3.7 per cent after reporting profit growth for the latest quarter that fell short of analysts’ expectations. All told, the S&P 500 rose 56.68 points to 7,165.08. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 79.61 to 49,230.71, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 398.09 to 24,836.60.



In the bond market, Treasury yields eased as traders upped their bets on the possibility that the Federal Reserve could resume its cuts to interest rates later this year. Related Article World markets How bad is the energy crisis? Three factors are pushing the world towards the cliff edge The path appeared to clear Friday for Trump’s nominee to chair the Fed, Kevin Warsh, after the US Justice Department ended its probe into the Fed’s current chair, Jerome Powell. Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, has said he would oppose Warsh until the investigation was resolved, effectively blocking his confirmation. Warsh is the choice of Trump, who has been arguing loudly for lower interest rates, which could help mortgages and other kinds of loans become less expensive. Shots were fired as accused gunman tried to storm the ballroom at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner in Washington on Sunday, resulting in Trump being hurried off the stage and guests ducking for cover beneath their tables.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury dipped to 4.30 per cent from 4.34 per cent late Thursday. A report in the morning also said sentiment among US consumers remains sour. A survey by the University of Michigan found weaker sentiment in April across political party, income, age, and education, though it improved a bit after the ceasefire in the war with Iran was announced earlier in the month. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1 per cent, and France’s CAC 40 fell 0.8 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves.
